nameStory: Hybocodon prolifer doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists stick with its scientific name. The genus name 'Hybocodon' comes from Greek words meaning 'hump' and 'bell,' referring to the bell-shaped body of its jellyfish stage. The species name 'prolifer' means 'bearing offspring,' highlighting this hydroid's remarkable ability to bud new jellyfish from its tentacles.
description: Hybocodon prolifer is a tiny marine hydroid that lives a double life, existing both as a small polyp attached to surfaces and as a free-swimming jellyfish. In its polyp stage, it looks like a miniature sea anemone with tentacles, typically just a few millimeters tall. The jellyfish stage is equally small, resembling a transparent bell with trailing tentacles. This fascinating creature can actually produce new jellyfish directly from its tentacles, making it one of nature's most efficient reproducers.

idTips.label: Budding jellyfish from tentacles
idTips.description: Look for tiny bell-shaped jellyfish budding directly from the swollen base of the single tentacle - this is unique among hydroids and feels almost magical to witness

idTips.label: Single beaded tentacle
idTips.description: The polyp has just one tentacle with a distinctive beaded or chain-like appearance, feeling slightly bumpy if gently touched

idTips.label: Transparent bell stage
idTips.description: The jellyfish stage appears as a crystal-clear, jelly-like bell that pulses gently through the water

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: Both stages are extremely small - you'll need to look closely or use a magnifying glass to see the intricate details

idTips.label: Attached polyp base
idTips.description: The polyp stage is firmly attached to hard surfaces like rocks, shells, or dock pilings

habitat: Hybocodon prolifer can be found in New England's coastal waters, typically attached to hard surfaces in harbors, tide pools, and shallow marine environments. Look for the polyp stage on dock pilings, rocks, shells, and other submerged structures in protected bays and estuaries. The jellyfish stage drifts in the same coastal waters, often near where the polyps are growing.

seasonality.spring: Polyps begin active growth and reproduction as water temperatures rise, with the first jellyfish buds starting to appear on tentacles.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with abundant jellyfish production and both life stages readily observable in warm coastal waters.
seasonality.fall: Continued reproduction though slowing down, with mature colonies still producing jellyfish as temperatures begin to drop.
seasonality.winter: Activity greatly reduced in cold New England waters, though some polyps may persist in protected, deeper areas.

funFact: This tiny creature essentially gives birth through its mouth area - the new jellyfish bud from the same tentacle used for feeding, making it one of the few animals that literally eats and reproduces with the same body part!
confusionNotes: The polyp stage might be confused with other small hydroids, but remember the magic word 'prolifer' - if you see tiny jellyfish budding from a single beaded tentacle, you've found your Hybocodon. Most other hydroids have multiple tentacles and don't produce jellyfish in this unique way.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being first described by the famous naturalist Louis Agassiz in 1860, this species remains relatively unknown to most beachgoers because of its tiny size. It's found worldwide, making it one of the most widely distributed yet least noticed marine animals on Earth.
compareHints: Since Hybocodon prolifer is the only species in its genus found in New England waters, compare it to other tubulariid hydroids in the region. Unlike most relatives that have multiple tentacles arranged in a crown, Hybocodon has just one distinctive beaded tentacle. The unique budding of jellyfish from the tentacle base, rather than from the body, sets it apart from all other local hydroids.
